chunks.text: 34-year-old male, Senior Official or Manager, resident of Sengkang, Singapore.
General Anesthesia with Laryngeal Mask Airway (LMA)

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Good morning, Mr./Ms./Mrs. [Patient's Name]. I'm [Provider's Name], the anesthesiologist who will be taking care of you during your surgery today. I just need to go through a few questions to make sure we're all set for your laparoscopic cholecystectomy under general anesthesia with an LMA. Is that okay with you?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Yes, of course. I want to make sure everything goes smoothly.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Great. Can you tell me a bit about your medical history, especially anything that might affect your anesthesia today?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Well, I have diabetes, high blood pressure, and I'm quite overweight. I take Metformin, Lisinopril, and Atorvastatin regularly. Oh, and I used to take Ranitidine for my stomach, but I stopped that a while back.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Thank you for sharing that. I see in your records that Ranitidine is still listed as active. Can you tell me more about when and why you stopped taking it?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Oh right, I stopped taking it about six months ago. My acid reflux got better, so I didn't need it anymore. I guess I didn't update the records properly.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: That's very helpful to know. Thank you for clarifying. Do you have any allergies, and have you ever had any reactions to medications or anesthesia in the past?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Yes, I'm allergic to penicillin. I had a rash the one time I took it. But I've never had surgery before, so no anesthesia history.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Got it. No previous anesthesia, and you're allergic to penicillin. That’s important. Now, regarding your current medications, are you taking all of them as prescribed, and have you taken them this morning?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Yes, I took my Metformin, Lisinopril, and Atorvastatin this morning with a sip of water. I didn’t eat anything else though, since I knew I had to fast.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Perfect, thank you. And just to confirm, you’ve had nothing to eat or drink since midnight?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Correct, nothing since last night. Just a bit of water with my meds this morning.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Excellent. Now, just a few more questions. How would you describe your overall energy level and ability to walk or climb stairs? This helps us understand your fitness for surgery.

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Hmm, I can walk around, but I do get a bit tired. I can’t run or anything, but I can manage daily activities. I’d say I’m moderately fit, lah.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Thanks for that. It gives me a good sense of your baseline. Lastly, do you have any concerns or questions about the anesthesia or the surgery itself?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: No, I think I’m all set. I just want to get this done and feel better.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Great, thank you so much for going through all that with me. We’ll take good care of you today. I’ll be with you the whole time and make sure you’re comfortable and safe.

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate it.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:00] induction propofol one hundred twenty milligrams

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:02] tube in, grade one view

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:05] iv fluids normal saline one liter to run at one hundred fifty ml per hour

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:10] increase sevoflurane to two percent due to increased blood pressure

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:20] administered morphine one milligram for pain management

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:25] patient's heart rate increased to one hundred ten, gave esmolol five milligrams

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Hi there, how are you feeling now after the surgery?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: I'm feeling a bit groggy, but okay. My tummy is sore, though.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Understandable. Can you tell me your pain level out of 10?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Eh, maybe around 4 or 5? It's manageable, I think.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Good. Are you feeling nauseous or have any vomiting since waking up?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: No nausea, thank goodness. I hate throwing up.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Excellent. How's your breathing? Any discomfort or tightness in your chest?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Breathing is fine, no problem there.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Great. Do you remember anything from the time you went into the operating room?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Nope, everything's blank until now. I don't recall a thing.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: That's normal with general anesthesia. Given your diabetes and high blood pressure, are you having any dizziness or vision changes?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: No dizziness, and vision seems okay. Just a bit tired, that's all.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Good to hear. We'll keep monitoring your vitals and sugar levels. Let the nurse know if you need anything.

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Will do, thank you. Hope to go home soon.

No recent cardiac evaluation or echocardiogram has been performed prior to surgery

ASA-PS Class III (patient has severe systemic disease affecting the respiratory, cardiovascular, or renal systems, but is still able to perform light physical activity)

At 08:00, propofol 120 milligrams was administered for induction.
At 08:02, tube was inserted with a grade one view.
At 08:05, normal saline 1000 milliliters was administered to run at 150 ml per hour.
At 08:10, sevoflurane was increased to 2% due to increased blood pressure.
At 08:20, morphine 1 milligram was administered for pain management.
At 08:25, patient's heart rate increased to 110.

Increased risk of Post-Operative Nausea and Vomiting (PONV) due to multiple factors including history of GERD, use of opioids (morphine), and sevoflurane anesthesia.
Airway watch due to history of GERD and use of Laryngeal Mask Airway (LMA), which may increase risk of aspiration or airway complications post-operatively.
Glycemic control monitoring necessary due to Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, as surgical stress and perioperative medications can affect blood glucose levels.
Analgesia management considering the patient's opioid dose (morphine) during surgery and potential for inadequate pain control or over-sedation post-operatively.
Hemodynamic watch due to Hypertension and the intraoperative increase in blood pressure requiring sevoflurane adjustment, as well as the administration of esmolol for tachycardia.
Risk of respiratory complications due to Obesity (as indicated in medical history) and the use of LMA, which may lead to difficulties in ventilation or oxygenation post-operatively.
34-year-old male undergoing elective Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy with General Anesthesia via Laryngeal Mask Airway (LMA).

Patient has Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, Hypertension, and a history of GERD. Medications include Metformin, Lisinopril, Atorvastatin, and was previously on Ranitidine which was discontinued. Allergic to Penicillin.
Intraoperative events include increased BP managed with sevoflurane, tachycardia managed with esmolol, and morphine administered for pain. NPO status confirmed.

Watch for Post-Operative Nausea and Vomiting (PONV), Airway complications, Glycemic control issues, Analgesia management challenges, Hemodynamic instability, and Respiratory complications due to Obesity and LMA use.
Patient reports feeling a bit groggy but okay with soreness in the abdominal area.
Patient reports pain level of 4 or 5 out of 10, describing it as manageable.
Patient denies any nausea or vomiting since waking up.
Patient reports no breathing difficulties, discomfort, or tightness in the chest.
Patient has no recall of events from the time of entering the operating room until waking up, which is consistent with general anesthesia.
Patient denies any dizziness or vision changes, but reports feeling tired, which is being monitored in the context of diabetes and hypertension.
